content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper explores the phrase structure induction, a key venue of syntactic study in NLP community, from the view of visual and audio sources.
They first segment the input speech into word sequence, and then use the Audio-Visual Neural Syntax Learner (AV-NSL) to perform grammar induction.


Generally, I think the key novelty lies in the introduction of the Audio-Visual grammar induction task, which is new and interesting to me. However, I'm more afraid there are some key issues that prevent me from giving a high evaluation.


The overall innovation and contribution could be somehow limited. The model framework is mostly borrowed from the existing VG-NSL (except the segment insertion part with minor improvement), and the task dataset is off-the-shelf. So I am wondering if there are enough contributions to meet the bar of ICLR.


From the technical perspective, also some concerns can be effortlessly found.

1. It is heavily a pipeline process, i.e., the image source -> object detection -> object proposal representations, and audio -> word/waveform segmentation -> syntax structure.

2. The overall performance is pretty much dependent on the quality of the word/waveform segmentation step. How much does this step affect grammar induction? About the proposed segment insertion, the authors propose inserting a short word segment in the sufficiently long gap only -- while I think this is problematic, because there're always some words not explicitly contained in the spoken audio (ellipsis in spoken language).

3. Regarding the efficiency of the audio processing, the system does not process grammar induction until reading and segmenting the whole speech.
And this two-stage practice is efficiency-unfriendly. In textual grammar induction, the tree construction performs tree induction incrementally along with the text reading without any latency.

4. Another key problem is the induction itself. It seems the tree induction is accomplished only by relying on the audio input, while leaving the image source for merely the alignment between the visual object and textual phrase. This way, the alignment learning contributes less to main grammar induction.
My suggestion is to encourage the visual information to also aid the grammar induction with visual semantics.

5. The success of the tree/grammar induction not only lies in the structure construction, but more relies on the text recognition (from audio segment (syllable) to the surface word), that is, the ASR. How to ensure ASR performances?

6.  Lack of task definition. How is the formal formulation of the inputs, and outputs? Does the grammar induction include the phrasal label (e.g., NP, VP) prediction? 


Overall, I feel strongly this paper should be enhanced further in terms of the technical novelty and paper writing up (some details are missing).

content.title: Response to Reviewer #PMHU
content.comment:
Thanks for your time and effort in reviewing our paper! We would like to clarify several points below:

> It is heavily a pipeline process, i.e., the image source -> object detection -> object proposal representations ...

We would like to clarify that we did not have any object detector involved in the pipeline (Figure 2), instead, we use global image representations following [1]. 

> ... I think this is problematic, because there're always some words not explicitly contained in the spoken audio (ellipsis in spoken language).

We agree that there may be ellipsis in spoken languages, however, the dataset we experimented with, SpokenCOCO, is constructed by having annotators reading textual image captions. All spoken captions should exactly correspond to their parallel text captions. While it's cleaner than the real-world data and arguably easier to deal with, we don't think the spoken captions will intentionally omit any word.

> In textual grammar induction, the tree construction performs tree induction incrementally along with the text reading without any latency.

To the best of our knowledge, most of the grammar induction or unsupervised parsing work on text requires seeing the whole sentence [2, 3, 4, *inter alia*]. We'd appreciate it a lot if you could point out some literature that does incremental grammar induction. 

> ... the alignment between the visual object and textual phrase. This way, the alignment learning contributes less to main grammar induction. My suggestion is to encourage the visual information to also aid the grammar induction with visual semantics.

As clarified above, we are not learning any alignment between visual *objects* and *textual* phrases, instead and in the same spirit as [1], our model learns visual semantics by matching global-image representations and speech spans. 

> The success of the tree/grammar induction not only lies in the structure construction, but more relies on the text recognition (from audio segment (syllable) to the surface word), that is, the ASR. How to ensure ASR performances?

We are sorry for not being clear enough at this point. As mentioned above, we use the SpokenCOCO dataset, which is constructed by reading MSCOCO caption text; that is, our spoken utterances have associated ground-truth text so that we do not need an external ASR system. 

> Does the grammar induction include the phrasal label (e.g., NP, VP) prediction? 

Following [1], we focus on unlabeled unsupervised constituency parsing of speech in this work. We will make it clearer in the revisions.

We will be working to improve the clarity of this paper. 


[1] https://aclanthology.org/P19-1180.pdf

[2] https://aclanthology.org/P02-1017.pdf

[3] https://aclanthology.org/N19-1114.pdf

[4] https://aclanthology.org/P19-1228.pdf

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to learn word segmentation and induce phrase structures in an unsupervised manner directly from speech audio signal in combination with accompanying visual inputs. Compared to past work, this setting aims to more closely mimic human language acquisition by using speech (as opposed to text) and multi-modal signal (as opposed to language alone). The introduction of this speech+vision setting for structure induction is the primary contribution of the work.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Speech+vision is a compelling setting for trying to capture some of the key elements of human language acquisition. I am unaware of past work that has incorporated all elements of this multi-modal setting, and this paper puts it on the map of viable settings for the study of phrase structure induction
- The paper takes the appropriate elements from the literature on each individual modality and slice of the full setting that has been studied in the literature.

Weaknesses:

My main critique of the work has to do with the fact that the proposed method doesn't seem to be all that effective at inducing phrase structures. For example, it fails to outperform a right-branching baseline. In all fairness the other neural methods perform even worse, but this still casts a cloud of doubt over whether the method is doing any meaningful non-random phrase structure induction at all, at least at the multi-word level.

When it comes to the claim that the model is "without inductive biases favoring any specific type of trees", this claim is sadly not proven in the paper. It is all too easy for a bias towards right-branching trees to sneak into an approach, even without the authors being necessarily aware of it. Outperforming the right-branching baseline provides some defense against this criticism, because at least then a branching bias can't be *all* that is happening with such a method. A more thorough way of addressing this issue would be to evaluate on multiple languages with different topological characteristics. If the same method competes with a right-branching baseline for English but *also* competes with e.g. a left-branching baseline for Japanese, that would be evidence that a strict right-branching bias has not inadvertently been introduced into the model.

The improvement over prior work on word segmentation (Table 1) also has some caveats. Most of the gains seem to be coming from MBR, which is included in the proposed method but not for any of the baselines. The remaining gap (e.g. VG-HuBERT vs. the proposed method in Table 1) might be entirely attributable to the segment insertion technique. While both of these improvements are a contribution of the present work, they don't really strike at the heart of the paper's motivation, which is leveraging multi-modality and having more naturalistic language acquisition.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Phrase structure induction from speech+images is a novel setting, and expands beyond the individual modality and task slices that have been used in prior work. The paper is also quite clear in its description of the methods and results.

A few minor points on clarity:
- In section 3.4, it would help to repeat that MBR is used to select between hyperparameters and model checkpoints (as opposed to, given a fixed model, using MBR to select among the exponentially many phrase structure trees that the single model could assign scores to)
- In section 4.4, it would help to clarify when single-round MBR would be too expensive. It seems viable for the purposes of Table 1, so it would help to explain how the conditions in Table 1 differ from the conditions where only 2-round MBR is feasible.
content.summary_of_the_review: On the one hand, language learning with visually-grounded speech is a promising research area, and modern methods have made it viable to start making progress in this space. Introducing phrase-structure induction in this setting is a novel contribution of the paper. On the other hand, the collection of entirely reasonable techniques that has been assembled to perform this task doesn't seem to have made much progress over the baseline. When it comes to methodology in the paper that is actually effective, I would point to MBR decoding and segment insertion (both of which are narrower in scope/novelty/impact compared to claims of gains from multi-modality). I interpret this paper as proposing a research problem that is viable to work on, combined with a method that doesn't actually work all that well -- all while the text claims that the method is effective. Ultimately this incongruity is what I base my recommendation on: there are several elements here that are individually compelling (e.g. the task proposal, effectiveness of MBR to remove all supervision, segment insertion technique, SAIoU metric), but the overall narrative and overarching theme of the paper doesn't quite fit.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #8ru5
content.comment:
Thanks for your time and effort in reviewing our paper! We appreciate your comments and suggestions.

> When it comes to the claim that the model is "without inductive biases favoring any specific type of trees", this claim is sadly not proven in the paper ...

We completely agree that our model may have implicit bias learned itself, and we are sorry for not being clear enough at this point. By the "no inductive biases" statement, we meant that the AV-NSL model does not have any explicit and manually designed components to favor right-branching trees, unlike the head-initial bias in VG-NSL [1] and biased tree decoding algorithms used in some text-based unsupervised parsing work [2]. We will make this clearer in future revisions. 

We will be working on improving the paper following your suggestions.

[1] https://aclanthology.org/P19-1180.pdf

[2] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.09428.pdf

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper conducts phrase structure induction from visually-grounded speech. The main contribution is that the proposed model is free of intermediate text or text pre-trained models. The paper proposes an audio-visual word segmentation method to recover the function word, a self training procedure, and a MBR decoding method. Experiments show that the proposed model infers meaningful phrase structures similar to those learned from naturally-supervised text parsing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. Instead of just leveraging VG-HuBERT, the proposed model adapts it to the specific task by placing short segments in long enough gaps.

2. The self-training process improves the accuracy, and the unsupervised decoding method is interesting.

3. The comparison of the proposed method with constructed baselines verify the effectiveness of proposed method.

Weakness:

1. It seems unclear that the application scenario of proposed method. Specifically, since ASR is usually accessible, we need to clarify the scenarios that we need to conduct phrase structure induction from visually grounded speech free of intermediate text or text pre-trained models. 

2. In my understanding, most components in the paper are from VG-NSL. Have you conducted ablation studies on the special designs such as audio-visual word segmentation (placing short segments in long enough gaps)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The topic studied in this paper is novel. The designs in paper mainly follow VG-NSL.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is novel and solid. However, the application and motivation for the work need to be better stated.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #z2zs
content.comment:
Thanks for your time and effort in reviewing our paper!

> It seems unclear that the application scenario of proposed method. Specifically, since ASR is usually accessible, we need to clarify the scenarios that we need to conduct phrase structure induction from visually grounded speech free of intermediate text or text pre-trained models.

We would like to clarify that our goal is to build a model that learns syntax directly from grounded speech; that is, our assumption is that we do not have any access to text to train an ASR model. Motivated by the fact that humans learn and use syntax before learning to read and write, we are interested in finding syntactic structures directly from speech.

While ASR systems have achieved decent performance on high-resource languages, they are not always available for low-resource languages; in addition, about 3,000 out of 7,000 languages all over the world do not have written forms. Besides its scientific contribution, our model may also help study these languages where ASR systems are not currently available or not even applicable.
